title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 140
paragraphs: The Ionians and Aiolians, as soon as the Lydians had been subdued by the Persians, sent messengers to Cyrus at Sardis, asking to be his subjects on the same terms as they had been subjects of Croesus. When he heard what they proposed to him, he spoke to them a fable, saying that a certain piper saw fishes in the sea and played on his pipe, supposing they would come out onto land; but being deceived in his expectation, he took a casting-net and enclosed a great multitude of fishes and drew them out of the water. When he saw them leaping about, he said to the fishes: “Stop your dancing now, I pray you, since you would not come out and dance before when I piped.” Cyrus spoke this fable to the Ionians and Aiolians for this reason: because the Ionians had refused to comply earlier, when Cyrus himself by a messenger had requested them to revolt from Croesus, while now, after the conquest had been made, they were ready to submit to Cyrus. He said this to them in anger. When the Ionians heard this answer brought back to their cities, they each put walls around them and gathered together at the Panionion, all except the Milesians, for with these alone Cyrus had sworn an agreement on the same terms the Lydians had granted. The rest of the Ionians resolved by common consent to send messengers to Sparta, to ask the Spartans to help the Ionians.
